answer.exemplar: The case for a closed form is that the amount of work it removes grows with the size of the problem, while the formula itself does not. Adding the squares one at a time up to 1000 needs 1000 additions and carries a running total that passes 333 million, and every one of those steps is another chance to slip; the closed form n times n plus 1 times 2n plus 1 over 6 gives 333833500 for n equal to 1000 in a single multiplication, and the identity behind it holds for every n rather than only for the sizes that have been tried. A closed form also earns its keep as a check: computing the same total two ways and finding they disagree tells you which of the two is wrong, whereas a single iterative answer has nothing to disagree with. The honest limit is that the derivation costs effort up front, so for a handful of terms the loop is quicker, and a formula misremembered is worse than no formula at all.

It should also note the checking role, since a closed form and an iteration can be run against each other and made to disagree, which is how an error in either gets caught. A weaker answer will only say the formula is faster, which is true but leaves out the second and more important use, which is that the two methods validate each other.
